question: Which level of the three-schema (ANSI/SPARC) architecture describes how data is physically stored on disk?
explanation: The internal (physical) level describes storage structures and access paths; the conceptual level describes the whole logical structure; external levels are user views.

question: Changing the conceptual (logical) schema without having to change external schemas or application programs is called:
explanation: Logical data independence protects views and applications from changes to the logical schema. Physical data independence protects the logical schema from changes to storage.

question: Which of the following is a Data Definition Language (DDL) command?
explanation: ALTER changes a schema object, so it is DDL. SELECT and UPDATE are DML; GRANT is DCL.

question: Which of the following are advantages of a DBMS over a traditional file-processing system? (Select all that apply.)
option_b: Controlled concurrent access by many users
explanation: A DBMS centralises data, controls concurrency and enforces constraints. It usually needs more hardware, and backups remain essential.

question: In the relational model, a row of a table is formally called a:
explanation: Rows are tuples, columns are attributes, and a domain is the set of allowed values for an attribute.

question: Explain the difference between a database schema and a database instance. Give one example of each for a Student table.
model_answer: A schema is the structure of the database: table names, attributes, types and constraints. It is defined at design time and changes rarely, e.g. Student(student_id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100), cgpa DECIMAL(3,2)). An instance (state) is the actual data stored at a particular moment, e.g. the rows (1, 'Ali', 3.40) and (2, 'Sara', 3.85). The instance changes with every insert, update or delete while the schema stays the same.
grading_rubric: 2 marks: Defines schema as the structure/description of the database that changes rarely; 2 marks: Defines instance as the data present at a given moment that changes frequently; 1 mark: Gives a correct example of each for Student

question: In Chen notation for ER diagrams, a weak entity set is drawn as a:
explanation: Weak entity sets use a double rectangle and their identifying relationship a double diamond. Dashed ellipses denote derived attributes.

question: A weak entity set is uniquely identified by:
option_a: A foreign key to any other entity set
option_b: Its partial key (discriminator) combined with the primary key of its identifying owner entity
explanation: A weak entity has no key of its own; its partial key is unique only within one owner, so the owner's key is added.

question: When mapping a binary many-to-many (M:N) relationship to relational tables, the relationship is usually represented as:
option_a: A foreign key in the table on either side
option_b: An extra attribute in one entity table
option_c: A separate table whose primary key combines the primary keys of both participating entities
option_d: It cannot be represented in the relational model
explanation: An M:N relationship needs its own table (e.g. Enrollment(student_id, course_id)); a single foreign key column cannot hold many values.

question: An attribute such as Age that can be computed from DateOfBirth is called a:
explanation: Derived attributes are calculated from other stored attributes and are shown as dashed ellipses.

question: Which statements about total participation of an entity set in a relationship are true? (Select all that apply.)
option_a: It is drawn with a double line between the entity set and the relationship in Chen notation
option_b: It means the relationship must be one-to-one
option_c: Every entity in the set must take part in at least one relationship instance
option_d: A weak entity set always has total participation in its identifying relationship
option_e: It means the entity set has no primary key
explanation: Total participation is about existence dependency, not cardinality. Weak entities cannot exist without their owner, so their participation is total.

question: Department (1) has many Employees (N). When mapping this 1:N relationship to tables, where should the foreign key go?
option_a: In both tables, referencing each other
option_b: In the Employee table, referencing Department
option_c: Only in a separate relationship table
option_d: In the Department table, referencing Employee
explanation: The foreign key goes on the N side: each employee row stores one dept_id. Putting it in Department would need many values per row.

question: Design an ER model for a university library: members borrow books; a book title can have several physical copies; each loan records the borrow date, due date and return date. Identify the entities (with keys), relationships, cardinalities and participation, and map the design to relational tables.
model_answer: Entities: Member(member_id PK, name, email); Book(isbn PK, title, author, publisher); Copy(copy_no, isbn) as a weak entity of Book with partial key copy_no, or a strong entity with copy_id PK; Loan as an entity or associative relationship with loan_id PK, borrow_date, due_date, return_date (nullable). Relationships: Book 1:N Copy (each copy belongs to exactly one book; total participation of Copy); Member 1:N Loan; Copy 1:N Loan (over time a copy is lent many times; at most one open loan at a time, enforced by a rule). Tables: Member(member_id, name, email); Book(isbn, title, author, publisher); Copy(isbn FK, copy_no, PK(isbn, copy_no)); Loan(loan_id, member_id FK, isbn, copy_no, FK(isbn, copy_no) -> Copy, borrow_date, due_date, return_date). Constraint: due_date >= borrow_date and return_date IS NULL OR return_date >= borrow_date.
grading_rubric: 2 marks: Identifies Member, Book, Copy and Loan with suitable primary keys; 2 marks: Separates Book (title) from Copy (physical item), e.g. as a weak entity; 2 marks: Correct cardinalities and participation for Book-Copy, Member-Loan and Copy-Loan; 3 marks: Correct relational mapping with foreign keys, including the composite key for Copy if weak; 1 mark: Places borrow, due and return dates on the loan, not on Member or Book

question: A minimal superkey (one with no redundant attributes) is called a:
explanation: A superkey uniquely identifies tuples; a candidate key is a superkey from which no attribute can be removed.

question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has candidate keys {A} and {B, C}. How many prime attributes does R have?
explanation: Prime attributes belong to at least one candidate key: A, B and C. D is non-prime.

question: Which integrity rule states that no part of a primary key can be NULL?
explanation: Entity integrity requires primary key values to be non-null; referential integrity governs foreign keys.

question: Which statements about foreign keys are true? (Select all that apply.)
option_a: A table can have only one foreign key
option_b: A foreign key column may contain NULL unless it is declared NOT NULL
option_c: A foreign key can reference the same table it is defined in
option_d: Foreign key values must be unique within their table
option_e: A foreign key must reference a primary key or unique (candidate) key of the referenced table
explanation: Self-referencing keys (e.g. manager_id -> emp_id) are allowed, a table can have many foreign keys, and foreign key values usually repeat.

question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has exactly one candidate key, {A}. How many superkeys does R have?
explanation: Every superkey must contain A; each of B, C and D may be included or not, giving 2^3 = 8 superkeys.

question: The cardinality of a relation is the number of its:
explanation: Cardinality counts tuples; degree (arity) counts attributes.

question: Which relational algebra operation returns only the rows (tuples) that satisfy a condition?
explanation: Selection filters rows; projection keeps chosen columns.

question: Relation R has 3 tuples and relation S has 4 tuples. How many tuples are in the Cartesian product R x S?
explanation: A Cartesian product pairs every tuple of R with every tuple of S: 3 x 4 = 12.

question: Which relational algebra operator directly answers 'for all' queries, such as 'find students who have taken every course'?
explanation: R / S returns the values in R associated with every tuple of S, which matches 'for all' conditions.

question: Which of the following can be expressed using only the basic operators selection, projection, Cartesian product, union, set difference and rename? (Select all that apply.)
option_a: Recursive transitive closure of a relation
option_b: Aggregation such as SUM or COUNT
explanation: Join, intersection (R - (R - S)) and division are derived operators. Aggregation needs an extended algebra, and transitive closure needs recursion.

question: Two relations are union-compatible when they:
option_c: Have the same degree and compatible domains for corresponding attributes
option_d: Have the same number of tuples
explanation: Union, intersection and difference need the same number of attributes with matching domains, position by position.

question: Given Student(sid, name), Enrolled(sid, cid) and Course(cid, title, dept), write a relational algebra expression for the names of students enrolled in at least one course offered by the 'CS' department. Explain each step.
model_answer: pi_name( Student JOIN Enrolled JOIN sigma_dept='CS'(Course) ). Steps: select CS courses from Course; natural join with Enrolled on cid to get the sids enrolled in those courses; natural join with Student on sid; project name. Selecting before joining keeps the intermediate results small. Equivalent: pi_name(Student JOIN pi_sid(Enrolled JOIN pi_cid(sigma_dept='CS'(Course)))).
grading_rubric: 2 marks: Applies selection dept = 'CS' to Course; 2 marks: Joins Course, Enrolled and Student on cid and sid correctly; 1 mark: Projects name as the final result

question: Which SQL statement removes a table, including its structure, from the database?
explanation: DELETE and TRUNCATE remove rows but keep the table definition; REMOVE TABLE is not SQL.

question: A foreign key is declared with ON DELETE CASCADE. What happens when a referenced parent row is deleted?
option_a: The child rows that reference it are deleted as well
option_b: Nothing happens to the child rows
option_d: The child foreign key values are set to NULL
explanation: CASCADE propagates the delete. Rejecting is NO ACTION/RESTRICT; setting NULL is ON DELETE SET NULL.

question: Which constraints can be declared inside a standard SQL CREATE TABLE statement? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE, CHECK and FOREIGN KEY (plus NOT NULL) are table constraints. GROUP BY is a query clause.

question: Which statement about UNIQUE and PRIMARY KEY constraints is correct?
option_a: They are identical in every respect
option_b: A PRIMARY KEY column may contain duplicate values
option_c: A UNIQUE column can never contain NULL
option_d: A table can have several UNIQUE constraints but only one PRIMARY KEY
explanation: A primary key is unique and NOT NULL, and there is one per table. UNIQUE columns generally allow NULL.

question: Which data type is most appropriate for storing an exact monetary amount such as 1499.99?
explanation: DECIMAL/NUMERIC stores exact values. FLOAT and REAL are approximate binary types that cause rounding errors with money.

question: What is the main difference between DELETE FROM t; and TRUNCATE TABLE t;?
option_a: TRUNCATE can delete only rows that match a condition
option_c: DELETE also removes the table definition
option_d: TRUNCATE removes all rows at once with no WHERE clause and is usually faster; DELETE removes rows one by one and accepts a WHERE clause
explanation: Both keep the table. TRUNCATE empties the whole table with minimal logging; DELETE can filter rows and fires row-level triggers.

question: Which SQL clause filters individual rows before any grouping takes place?
explanation: WHERE filters rows before GROUP BY; HAVING filters groups afterwards.

question: Tables: Department(dept_id, dept_name) has 5 rows, 2 of which have no employees. Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id) has 10 rows, each with a valid dept_id. How many rows does SELECT * FROM Department d LEFT JOIN Employee e ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id; return?
explanation: Each of the 10 employees matches one department (10 rows) and the 2 departments with no employees appear once each with NULLs (2 rows): 12.

question: Using Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id), which condition correctly finds employees who have no manager (manager_id is NULL)?
explanation: Any comparison with NULL using = yields UNKNOWN, so no rows match. IS NULL is required.

question: Using Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id), which query lists each employee's name together with their manager's name?
option_a: SELECT e.name, m.name FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON e.emp_id = m.emp_id;
option_c: SELECT e.name, m.name FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON e.manager_id = m.manager_id;
option_d: SELECT e.name, m.name FROM Employee e JOIN Employee m ON e.manager_id = m.emp_id;
explanation: A self join matches each employee's manager_id to the manager's emp_id. The other joins pair employees with themselves or with colleagues.

question: Which keyword removes duplicate rows from a SELECT result?
explanation: SELECT DISTINCT removes duplicates; ALL (the default) keeps them.

question: Using Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id), which WHERE clauses return employees whose name starts with the letter A? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: % matches any sequence and _ exactly one character, so 'A_' matches only two-letter names and '%A' matches names ending in A. * is not a SQL wildcard.

question: How does UNION differ from UNION ALL?
option_a: UNION ALL removes duplicate rows; UNION keeps them
option_b: UNION ALL sorts the result automatically
option_c: UNION requires the same table on both sides
option_d: UNION removes duplicate rows from the combined result; UNION ALL keeps them
explanation: UNION performs duplicate elimination, which costs extra work; UNION ALL simply appends the results.

question: Using Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id), which ORDER BY sorts by department ascending and, within each department, by salary from highest to lowest?
option_d: ORDER BY dept_id ASC DESC salary
explanation: Sort keys apply left to right, each with its own direction; ASC is the default.

question: Using Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id) and Department(dept_id, dept_name), write an SQL query that lists every department name with its number of employees, including departments with zero employees, sorted from the largest to the smallest department.
model_answer: SELECT d.dept_name, COUNT(e.emp_id) AS employee_count FROM Department d LEFT JOIN Employee e ON e.dept_id = d.dept_id GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name ORDER BY employee_count DESC; -- COUNT(e.emp_id) gives 0 for empty departments, while COUNT(*) would wrongly give 1.
grading_rubric: 2 marks: Uses a LEFT (or RIGHT) OUTER JOIN so departments without employees appear; 1 mark: Counts e.emp_id (not COUNT(*)) so empty departments show 0; 1 mark: Groups by the department correctly; 1 mark: Orders by the count in descending order

question: Which SQL clause filters groups after aggregation, for example to keep only departments with more than 5 employees?
explanation: HAVING applies conditions to groups, so it can use aggregates such as COUNT(*) > 5.

question: Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id) has 10 rows, and 3 of them have salary NULL. What does SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(salary) FROM Employee; return?
explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values.

question: Using Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id), which query finds employees who earn more than the average salary?
option_a: SELECT name FROM Employee HAVING salary > AVG(salary);
option_b: SELECT name FROM Employee WHERE salary > AVG(salary);
option_c: SELECT name FROM Employee WHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employee);
option_d: SELECT name FROM Employee WHERE AVG(salary) < salary GROUP BY name;
explanation: Aggregates cannot appear directly in WHERE, so the average must come from a subquery.

question: Using Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id), at least one employee in department 3 has salary NULL. What does SELECT name FROM Employee WHERE salary NOT IN (SELECT salary FROM Employee WHERE dept_id = 3); return?
option_a: All employees whose salary differs from every department 3 salary
option_b: Only the employees whose salary is NULL
explanation: x NOT IN (..., NULL) is never TRUE: it evaluates to FALSE or UNKNOWN. Use NOT EXISTS or filter NULLs out of the subquery.

question: A correlated subquery is one that:
option_a: Can appear only in the FROM clause
option_c: Runs only once regardless of the outer query
option_d: Refers to a column of the outer query, so it is logically evaluated once for each outer row
explanation: Correlation means the inner query depends on the current outer row, e.g. WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id.

question: Which aggregate expressions ignore NULL values? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: All aggregates over a column skip NULLs. COUNT(*) counts rows regardless of their values.

question: Using Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id), which query returns the second-highest distinct salary?
option_a: SELECT salary FROM Employee WHERE salary = MAX(salary) - 1;
option_b: SELECT MIN(salary) FROM (SELECT salary FROM Employee) t;
option_c: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee ORDER BY salary DESC;
option_d: SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM Employee);
explanation: The highest salary below the overall maximum is the second-highest distinct value.

question: Which statement about the EXISTS operator is true?
option_a: EXISTS cannot be used with correlated subqueries
option_b: EXISTS compares a value against a list of values
option_c: EXISTS returns the number of rows in the subquery
option_d: EXISTS is TRUE if its subquery returns at least one row
explanation: EXISTS tests for non-emptiness and is most often used with a correlated subquery.

question: Using Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id), write an SQL query that returns, for each department, the employee or employees with the highest salary in that department. Your query must handle ties.
model_answer: SELECT e.dept_id, e.name, e.salary FROM Employee e WHERE e.salary = (SELECT MAX(e2.salary) FROM Employee e2 WHERE e2.dept_id = e.dept_id); Alternative: SELECT dept_id, name, salary FROM (SELECT dept_id, name, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM Employee) t WHERE rnk = 1; Both return every employee tied for the top salary. ROW_NUMBER() or LIMIT 1 would wrongly drop ties.
grading_rubric: 2 marks: Finds the maximum salary per department (correlated subquery, join to grouped maxima, or window function); 2 marks: Returns the matching employee rows, not just the maximum value; 1 mark: Handles ties (avoids ROW_NUMBER or LIMIT 1)

question: A relation is in First Normal Form (1NF) when:
option_a: Every determinant is a candidate key
option_c: Every attribute holds only atomic (indivisible) values
explanation: 1NF forbids repeating groups and multivalued cells. The other options describe 3NF, 2NF and BCNF.

question: A relation in Second Normal Form (2NF) has no:
option_b: Partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on part of a candidate key
option_d: Transitive dependency of a non-prime attribute on a key
explanation: 2NF = 1NF plus every non-prime attribute fully dependent on each candidate key. Transitive dependencies are removed by 3NF.

question: Relation R(A, B, C) has functional dependencies A -> B and B -> C, and A is the only candidate key. What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
explanation: The key is a single attribute, so there are no partial dependencies (2NF). B -> C is a transitive dependency of the non-prime C, so R is not in 3NF.

question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has functional dependencies AB -> C, C -> D and D -> A. What are all the candidate keys of R?
explanation: B never appears on a right-hand side, so it is in every key, but B+ = {B}. AB+, BC+ (C->D->A, then AB->C) and BD+ (D->A, then AB->C) are all ABCD, and each is minimal.

question: Relation R(A, B, C, D) has functional dependencies AB -> C, C -> D and D -> A (candidate keys AB, BC and BD). What is the highest normal form R satisfies?
explanation: Every attribute is prime, so every dependency satisfies 3NF. C -> D violates BCNF because C is not a superkey.

question: Relation R(A, B, C, D, E) has functional dependencies A -> B, B -> C and CD -> E. What is the attribute closure {A, D}+?
explanation: Start with AD; A -> B adds B; B -> C adds C; CD -> E adds E.

question: Which anomalies does normalization aim to reduce? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: Redundant storage causes insertion, update and deletion anomalies. The other two are not standard terms.

question: A decomposition of R into R1 and R2 is a lossless-join decomposition if:
option_a: R1 and R2 have no attributes in common
option_c: Both R1 and R2 are in BCNF
option_d: The common attributes (R1 intersect R2) functionally determine all attributes of R1 or all attributes of R2
explanation: If the shared attributes form a superkey of either part, joining R1 and R2 recreates R exactly. Dependency preservation is a separate property.

question: Which statement about BCNF and 3NF is correct?
option_a: Every relation in BCNF is also in 3NF, but not every 3NF relation is in BCNF
option_b: BCNF allows transitive dependencies of non-prime attributes
option_c: Every relation in 3NF is also in BCNF
explanation: BCNF is stricter: it requires every determinant to be a superkey. 3NF also allows X -> A when A is prime.

question: StudentCourse(StudentID, StudentName, CourseID, CourseTitle, InstructorID, InstructorName, Grade) has the functional dependencies StudentID -> StudentName; CourseID -> CourseTitle, InstructorID; InstructorID -> InstructorName; and (StudentID, CourseID) -> Grade. (a) Identify the candidate key. (b) State the highest normal form and justify it. (c) Decompose the relation into 3NF, stating the keys of each new relation.
model_answer: (a) The candidate key is (StudentID, CourseID): its closure contains every attribute and neither attribute alone does. (b) The relation is only in 1NF: StudentName depends on StudentID alone and CourseTitle and InstructorID depend on CourseID alone, which are partial dependencies on part of the key, so it is not in 2NF. (c) 3NF decomposition: Student(StudentID PK, StudentName); Course(CourseID PK, CourseTitle, InstructorID FK); Instructor(InstructorID PK, InstructorName); Enrollment(StudentID FK, CourseID FK, Grade, PK(StudentID, CourseID)). The InstructorName transitive dependency (CourseID -> InstructorID -> InstructorName) is removed by the separate Instructor table. The decomposition is lossless and preserves all dependencies.
grading_rubric: 2 marks: Identifies (StudentID, CourseID) as the candidate key; 2 marks: States 1NF and justifies it with the partial dependencies; 2 marks: Separates Student and Course to remove partial dependencies (2NF); 2 marks: Separates Instructor to remove the transitive dependency (3NF); 2 marks: Keeps Grade in an Enrollment relation with the correct composite key and foreign keys

question: Which ACID property ensures that a transaction is executed completely or not at all?
explanation: Atomicity means all-or-nothing; a failure rolls back any partial work.

question: Which ACID property guarantees that the changes of a committed transaction survive a system crash?
explanation: Durability is usually achieved by forcing the log to stable storage at commit.

question: A dirty read occurs when a transaction:
option_a: Overwrites data another transaction has already committed
option_b: Reads the same row twice and gets different committed values
option_c: Re-runs a query and sees new rows inserted by another transaction
option_d: Reads data written by another transaction that has not yet committed
explanation: The other options describe non-repeatable reads, phantom reads and overwrites (lost updates).

question: According to the SQL standard, what is the lowest isolation level that prevents non-repeatable reads?
explanation: READ COMMITTED prevents dirty reads only. REPEATABLE READ also prevents non-repeatable reads; SERIALIZABLE also prevents phantoms.

question: According to the SQL standard, which phenomena are still possible at the READ COMMITTED isolation level? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: READ COMMITTED only guarantees that you never read uncommitted data.

question: Which SQL statement undoes all changes made by the current transaction since it began?
explanation: ROLLBACK undoes the transaction's work (or back to a savepoint with ROLLBACK TO). REVOKE removes privileges.

question: Explain, using a bank transfer of Rs. 5,000 from account A to account B as an example, why the debit and credit must run inside a single transaction. Refer to atomicity, consistency and isolation in your answer.
model_answer: The transfer is two updates: A.balance = A.balance - 5000 and B.balance = B.balance + 5000. Atomicity: if the system fails after the debit but before the credit, money would disappear; running both in one transaction means either both are applied or both are rolled back. Consistency: the invariant that the total of A and B is unchanged (and balances stay non-negative, if constrained) holds before and after the transaction. Isolation: another transaction, such as a report summing all balances or a second transfer from A, must not see the intermediate state where A is debited but B not yet credited, and concurrent transfers must not cause lost updates on A.
grading_rubric: 2 marks: Atomicity: explains the partial-failure case and the all-or-nothing outcome; 1 mark: Consistency: states the invariant (total balance preserved); 2 marks: Isolation: explains the danger of other transactions seeing or overwriting intermediate values

question: Under two-phase locking (2PL), a transaction:
option_a: Must lock every item in the database before starting
option_b: Acquires locks during a growing phase and, once it releases any lock, cannot acquire new ones
option_c: Releases each lock immediately after using the item
explanation: 2PL splits a transaction into a growing phase and a shrinking phase; the lock point separates them.

question: Basic (non-strict) two-phase locking guarantees that schedules are:
explanation: 2PL ensures conflict serializability but can deadlock, and without strictness it can cause cascading aborts.

question: Consider the schedule r1(X), w2(X), w1(X), c1, c2, where r means read, w means write and c means commit. Is it conflict-serializable?
option_a: No, because the precedence graph has a cycle between T1 and T2
option_b: Yes, it is equivalent to the serial order T1, T2
option_c: It cannot be determined without the data values
option_d: Yes, it is equivalent to the serial order T2, T1
explanation: r1(X) before w2(X) gives T1 -> T2; w2(X) before w1(X) gives T2 -> T1. A cycle means not conflict-serializable.

question: Which statement about lock compatibility is correct?
option_a: Two shared (S) locks on the same item are compatible
option_b: An exclusive lock is compatible with any other lock
option_c: Two exclusive locks on the same item are compatible
option_d: A shared lock and an exclusive (X) lock on the same item are compatible
explanation: Many readers may hold S locks together; an X lock excludes every other lock.

question: Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until the transaction commits or aborts. What is its main benefit over basic 2PL?
option_b: It removes the need for a log
option_c: It allows more concurrency than basic 2PL
explanation: Because no one can read uncommitted writes, aborting one transaction never forces others to abort. Deadlocks are still possible.

question: Which of the following are valid techniques for handling deadlocks? (Select all that apply.)
option_d: Raising the isolation level to SERIALIZABLE
option_e: Wait-for graph detection with victim rollback
explanation: Wait-die and wound-wait prevent deadlocks with timestamps; wait-for graphs detect them; timeouts are a simple practical approach. A stricter isolation level usually adds locking and can make deadlocks more likely.

question: In multiversion concurrency control (MVCC), readers typically:
option_b: Read a consistent snapshot, so readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers
option_c: Must take an exclusive lock on every row they read
option_d: Block all writers until the read completes
explanation: MVCC keeps older row versions so each transaction reads the version valid for its snapshot.

question: T1 transfers 50 from A to B: R(A); A = A - 50; W(A); R(B); B = B + 50; W(B). T2 displays A + B: R(A); R(B); print(A + B). (a) Give an interleaved schedule in which T2 prints an incorrect total, and explain why. (b) Show how two-phase locking prevents this, stating which locks each transaction requests and where a transaction must wait.
model_answer: (a) Schedule: T1: R(A), W(A) [A reduced by 50]; T2: R(A), R(B), print(A + B); T1: R(B), W(B). T2 reads A after the debit but B before the credit, so it prints a total 50 less than the true total (an inconsistent analysis / unrepeatable state). (b) Under 2PL, T1 takes X(A) before writing A. T2 requests S(A) and must wait because S and X conflict. T1 cannot release X(A) until it has acquired all its locks, including X(B) (growing phase); under strict 2PL it releases at commit. After T1 releases, T2 gets S(A) and S(B) and reads both committed values, printing the correct total. Equivalently, if T2 locks first it holds S(A) and S(B) until it has read both, and T1 waits for X(A). The result is equivalent to a serial order.
grading_rubric: 3 marks: Gives a valid interleaving where T2 reads A after the debit and B before the credit; 2 marks: Explains why the printed total is wrong; 3 marks: Correctly states the S and X locks requested and where a transaction blocks; 2 marks: Explains that the growing/shrinking rule (or strict 2PL) yields a serializable outcome

question: The write-ahead logging (WAL) rule requires that:
option_a: Every transaction writes its log to a separate disk
option_b: Data pages are written to disk before their log records
option_c: The log record for an update is written to stable storage before the modified data page is written to disk
option_d: The log is written only after the transaction commits
explanation: WAL ensures there is always enough information to undo a change that reaches disk; the log must also be forced at commit.

question: In what order does the ARIES recovery algorithm perform its three phases after a crash?
explanation: Analysis finds dirty pages and active transactions, Redo repeats history, then Undo rolls back the transactions that did not commit.

question: Why does taking periodic checkpoints shorten crash recovery?
option_a: Checkpoints delete committed transactions from the database
option_b: Recovery only needs to process log records from around the most recent checkpoint instead of the whole log
explanation: A checkpoint records which transactions were active and flushes state, which bounds how far back recovery must scan.

question: A DBMS uses an undo/redo (steal, no-force) buffer policy. After a crash, which actions are required? (Select all that apply.)
option_a: Undo the updates of uncommitted transactions whose changes may already be on disk
option_b: Redo the updates of committed transactions whose changes may not have reached disk
option_c: Re-run all committed transactions from the application code
option_d: Delete the log once the database restarts
explanation: No-force means committed changes may be missing from disk (redo); steal means uncommitted changes may be on disk (undo).

question: A deferred-update (NO-UNDO/REDO) recovery scheme writes a transaction's changes to the database:
option_d: Never; changes stay in the log
explanation: Because nothing reaches the database before commit, undo is never needed, but committed work may need redo.

question: In a B+ tree index, where are the data records (or pointers to them) stored?
explanation: Internal nodes hold only routing keys; all entries live in the leaves.

question: Why are the leaf nodes of a B+ tree linked to their neighbouring leaves?
option_a: To speed up exact-match lookups on the root
option_b: To balance the tree after insertions
option_d: To make range queries and ordered scans efficient
explanation: After finding the start of a range, the scan follows sibling pointers instead of returning to the root.

question: Which type of index is well suited to equality lookups but unsuitable for range queries such as salary BETWEEN 50000 AND 80000?
explanation: Hashing scatters keys, so adjacent values are not stored together.

question: How many clustered indexes can a table have?
explanation: A clustered index defines the physical order of rows, and rows can be stored in only one order.

question: In which situations is adding an index likely to improve performance? (Select all that apply.)
option_b: A write-heavy log table that is almost never queried
option_c: A column frequently used in WHERE filters on a large table
option_d: A column used in JOIN conditions between large tables
option_e: A column used in ORDER BY when only the first few rows are fetched with LIMIT
explanation: Indexes speed up reads but cost space and slow down inserts and updates, so they help only where reads benefit.

question: In a B+ tree where every node (internal and leaf) holds about 100 entries, roughly how many levels are needed to index 1,000,000 keys?
explanation: 100 x 100 x 100 = 1,000,000, so a root, one internal level and a leaf level suffice. High fan-out keeps B+ trees shallow.

question: A composite index exists on (last_name, first_name). Which predicate can use it most efficiently?
explanation: A composite index is sorted by its leftmost column first, so a condition on last_name (the leftmost prefix) can seek into it.

question: Which heuristic does a query optimizer commonly apply when rewriting a query?
option_a: Always join the largest tables first
option_c: Postpone projections until the final step only
option_d: Apply selections as early as possible (push selections down)
explanation: Filtering early shrinks intermediate results, which reduces the cost of later joins.

question: What is the EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN PLAN) command used for?
option_a: Running a query in a transaction
option_c: Showing the execution plan the optimizer chooses for a query
option_d: Listing the privileges of a user
explanation: The plan shows access paths (scans or index seeks), join methods and estimated costs, which helps tuning.

question: Two large tables are joined on an equality condition. Neither has a useful index, and the smaller table fits in memory. Which join algorithm is usually the most efficient?
explanation: A hash join builds a hash table on the smaller input and probes it once per row of the larger input, in roughly linear time.

question: Why can WHERE YEAR(order_date) = 2026 be slower than WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01' AND order_date < '2027-01-01'?
option_a: The second form returns different rows
option_b: Applying a function to the column prevents the normal use of an index on order_date
explanation: The range predicate is sargable: the optimizer can seek in an index on order_date. Wrapping the column in a function usually forces a scan.

question: A (non-materialized) view in SQL is best described as:
option_a: A virtual table defined by a stored query
option_c: A physical copy of a table
explanation: A view stores the query, not the data; its rows are computed when it is used.

question: How does a materialized view differ from an ordinary view?
option_a: It cannot be queried with SELECT
option_c: It stores the query result physically and must be refreshed to reflect changes in the base tables
option_d: It is recomputed on every query
explanation: Materialized views trade freshness for speed, which suits expensive reporting queries.

question: A database trigger is:
option_a: A procedure that runs automatically in response to events such as INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE on a table
option_b: A constraint that can only check for NULL values
explanation: Triggers are commonly used for auditing, derived values and complex integrity rules.

question: Which are valid reasons to create a view? (Select all that apply.)
option_a: Restricting users to certain columns or rows
option_b: Simplifying a complex query for reuse
option_c: Guaranteeing that queries run faster than on the base tables
option_d: Providing logical data independence for applications
explanation: An ordinary view is expanded into its query, so it does not by itself make queries faster.

question: Using Employee(emp_id, name, dept_id, salary, manager_id) and an audit table SalaryAudit(emp_id, old_salary, new_salary, changed_at), write a trigger in any SQL dialect that records every change to an employee's salary.
model_answer: MySQL: CREATE TRIGGER trg_salary_audit AFTER UPDATE ON Employee FOR EACH ROW BEGIN IF NOT (NEW.salary <=> OLD.salary) THEN INSERT INTO SalaryAudit (emp_id, old_salary, new_salary, changed_at) VALUES (OLD.emp_id, OLD.salary, NEW.salary, NOW()); END IF; END; PostgreSQL: a trigger function that inserts OLD.emp_id, OLD.salary, NEW.salary, now() WHEN (OLD.salary IS DISTINCT FROM NEW.salary), attached with CREATE TRIGGER ... AFTER UPDATE OF salary ON Employee FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION log_salary_change(); The NULL-safe comparison ensures changes to or from NULL are also logged.
grading_rubric: 1 mark: Fires AFTER (or BEFORE) UPDATE on Employee; 1 mark: Is a row-level trigger (FOR EACH ROW); 2 marks: Inserts the OLD and NEW salary values and a timestamp into SalaryAudit; 1 mark: Logs only when the salary actually changes

question: What is the most effective defence against SQL injection?
option_c: Validating input only in the browser
option_d: Escaping quotes manually in user input
explanation: Parameters are sent separately from the SQL text, so input can never change the query's structure. The others are incomplete.

question: Which SQL command gives a user privileges on a database object?
explanation: GRANT gives privileges and REVOKE removes them; ALLOW and PERMIT are not SQL commands.

question: Which practices follow the principle of least privilege for a web application's database account? (Select all that apply.)
option_a: Grant only the SELECT, INSERT and UPDATE privileges the application needs on specific tables
option_b: Connect the application as the database superuser for simplicity
option_c: Revoke privileges that are no longer used
option_d: Share one administrator password among all developers
option_e: Use separate accounts for schema migrations and for the running application
explanation: Limiting each account to what it needs reduces the damage from a compromised application or credential.

question: How should user passwords be stored in a database?
option_b: Encrypted with a key stored in the same database
option_c: As salted hashes computed with a slow algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2
option_d: In plain text in a column only admins can read
explanation: Slow salted hashes resist brute force and rainbow tables. Reversible encryption and fast hashes like MD5 are unsafe.

question: An application logs users in with this code: query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "' AND password = '" + pwd + "'". (a) Show an input that lets an attacker log in without knowing the password. (b) Rewrite the login check safely.
model_answer: (a) Entering the email ' OR '1'='1' -- (or admin@example.com' --) produces SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '' OR '1'='1' --' AND password = '...'; the comment removes the password check and the OR condition is always true, so the first user (often the admin) is returned. (b) Use a parameterized query to fetch the user by email only, e.g. SELECT id, password_hash FROM users WHERE email = ?, binding email as a parameter; then verify the password in application code with a slow hash function such as bcrypt.compare(pwd, password_hash). Never build SQL with string concatenation, and never store plain-text passwords.
grading_rubric: 2 marks: Gives a working injection input and explains how it bypasses the password check; 2 marks: Uses a parameterized query or prepared statement with bound values; 1 mark: Checks a stored password hash instead of comparing plain-text passwords in SQL

question: According to the CAP theorem, when a network partition occurs a distributed system must choose between:
explanation: Partition tolerance is unavoidable in a distributed system, so during a partition it must give up either consistency or availability.

question: MongoDB is primarily an example of which kind of database?
explanation: MongoDB stores JSON-like (BSON) documents grouped into collections.

question: Which data model is best suited to highly connected data such as social networks and recommendation paths?
explanation: Graph databases store relationships as edges, so traversals such as friends-of-friends avoid many expensive joins.

question: Which properties make up the BASE model often used by NoSQL systems? (Select all that apply.)
explanation: BASE relaxes ACID-style guarantees in favour of availability and scalability.

question: Splitting a table's rows across several database servers, for example by customer region, is called:
explanation: Sharding distributes rows; replication copies the same data; vertical partitioning splits columns.

question: What is the main benefit of database replication?
option_b: Stronger consistency at no extra cost
option_c: Higher availability and the ability to spread read traffic across copies
explanation: Replicas survive node failures and serve reads, at the cost of extra storage and the work of keeping copies in sync.
